message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and federal law. If you need more detail on any point, let me know!

| # | Right / Protection | What it Means | Practical Tips |
|---|--------------------|---------------|----------------|
| **1** | **Security Deposit Limits** | Landlords may charge up to **one month’s rent** for an unfurnished unit and **two months’ rent** for a furnished unit. | Keep a copy of the lease and any deposit receipts. |
| **2** | **Deposit Return** | Landlord must return the security deposit within **30 days** after the tenant vacates, minus any lawful deductions. | Inspect the unit before moving out; document any damage with photos. |
| **3** | **Repair & Maintenance** | Landlord must keep the premises in a habitable condition—plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, etc. | Report needed repairs in writing (email or text) and keep copies. |
| **4** | **Habitability Standards** | The property must meet basic health and safety standards (e.g., functioning smoke detectors, no mold, safe locks). | If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct remedy. |
| **5** | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | Landlord cannot disturb your peaceful use of the premises. | Document any disturbances (noise, entry without notice). |
| **6** | **Notice Requirements for Entry** | Landlord must give **at least 24 hours’ written notice** before entering, except in emergencies. | Ask for a written notice (email or text) and keep a log of entries. |
| **7** | **Rent Increase Notice** | For month‑to‑month leases, landlords must give **30 days’ written notice** before raising rent. | Verify the notice is in writing and keep a copy. |
| **8** | **Lease Termination** | Tenants can terminate a lease by giving **30 days’ written notice** (for month‑to‑month) or following the lease’s specified termination clause. | Provide notice in writing and keep a copy. |
| **9** | **Discrimination Protections** | Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | Keep records of any discriminatory actions; you can file a complaint with HUD or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. |
| **10** | **Right to a Written Lease** | While not required for all leases, having a written lease clarifies terms and protects both parties. | Request a written lease if you’re signing a new agreement. |
| **11** | **Right to Withhold Rent** | If the landlord fails to make necessary repairs, you may withhold rent (up to the amount of the repair cost) after giving notice and allowing a reasonable period to fix the issue. | Keep receipts for repairs and document the landlord’s failure to comply. |
| **12** | **Right to Sue for Unlawful Eviction** | If you believe an eviction is unlawful (e.g., no proper notice, retaliation), you can file a lawsuit in the appropriate court. | Consult an attorney or tenant advocacy group for guidance. |
| **13** | **Right to a Refund of Overpaid Rent** | If you overpay rent or the landlord refuses to refund a security deposit, you can seek a refund through the court. | Keep all payment records and receipts. |
| **14** | **Right to a Fair Eviction Process** | Landlords must follow the legal eviction process: proper notice, filing a complaint, and obtaining a court order. | If you receive an eviction notice, review it carefully and consider legal counsel. |
| **15** | **Right to a Safe Environment** | Landlords must address hazards such as lead paint, asbestos, or pest infestations. | Report hazards promptly and keep documentation. |

### How to Protect Your Rights

1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of leases, notices, emails, texts, repair requests, and photos of the unit.
2. **Know the Law** – Familiarize yourself with the Texas Property Code sections relevant to your situation (e.g., §§ 92.001–92.021 for security deposits).
3. **Communicate in Writing** – Whenever possible, use email or text so you have a record.
4. **Seek Legal Advice** – If you face a dispute, consult a tenant rights organization or an attorney who specializes in landlord‑tenant law.
5. **File Complaints** – If you suspect discrimination or unlawful practices, file complaints with HUD or the Texas Commission on Human Rights.

---

#### Quick Reference: Texas Property Code Sections

| Section | Topic |
|---------|-------|
| § 92.001–92.021 | Security Deposits |
| § 92.101 | Habitability |
| § 92.111 | Notice of Entry |
| § 92.112 | Rent Increase Notice |
| § 92.113 | Lease Termination |
| § 92.114 | Discrimination |
| § 92.115 | Eviction Process |

Feel free to ask for more detail on any specific right or for help drafting a notice or complaint!
